407.title: The stained cloth
407.hook: a dirty cloth won't take the dye; a cleansed mind takes the good (MN 7)
407.howItsDone: In Theravada and other monastic communities, robes are dyed in shades of ochre, saffron or brown, and MN 7's image of washing before dyeing is used to describe clearing the mind's stains before cultivating the immeasurables.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhaya-bherava, and your line, face it where it finds you. When a small fear showed up, did you stay put for three breaths? Day four hundred seven.
screen: `BHAYA-BHERAVA — FACE IT WHERE IT FINDS YOU.`

segments.voice: Home dyers learn one rule the hard way, usually on a favorite shirt: wash it first. If there's grease or grime in the cotton, the color comes out patchy and dull, however good the dye is, and more dye won't fix it. You can't cover a stain with color. You have to take it out, and then the color holds. MN 7 uses this same picture for the mind. Today: the stained cloth.
screen: `WASH IT FIRST.` → `MORE DYE WON'T FIX IT.` → `THEN THE COLOR HOLDS.`

segments.voice: MN 7, the Vatthupama, the simile of the cloth. Suppose a cloth were stained and dirty, the Buddha says, and a dyer dipped it in blue, or yellow, or red, or crimson. It would come out badly dyed, impure in color. Why? Because the cloth wasn't clean. But dip a clean, bright cloth, and it takes the dye beautifully. In the same way, he says, when the mind is stained, an unhappy destination can be expected; when the mind is clean, a happy one. Then he names the stains, sixteen of them: covetousness, ill will, anger, revenge, contempt, domineering, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, rivalry, conceit, arrogance, vanity and negligence. It's an old list, and it could describe an ordinary week online. The key move is seeing a stain as a stain, and letting it go. Then the cloth is ready. And what color does it take? Confidence in the Buddha, the teaching and the community. Then the four immeasurables: loving-kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity, filling the world in every direction. The order matters. Not dye first and hope it covers. Clean first; then the color holds. The Dhammapada has a dyed-cloth verse too, in Max Müller's translation: “He who wishes to put on the yellow dress without having cleansed himself from sin” is not worthy of it, the verse goes on. The robe is the color. The washing comes first.
screen: `A STAINED CLOTH TAKES DYE BADLY.` · `SIXTEEN STAINS OF THE MIND.` · `SEE THE STAIN, LET IT GO.` · `CLEAN FIRST, THEN THE COLOR HOLDS.` · then, large: `CLEAN CLOTH TAKES DYE.`

segments.voice: Pick one stain from the list that you recognize: envy, maybe, or an old grudge, or vanity. Don't scrub at it. Just see it plainly, the way you'd hold a shirt up to the light and say: there's the mark. On each out-breath, loosen your grip on it a little. Then, for the last part of the sit, let one color in: wish one person well. And after the bell, if you like, clean one real thing: a cup, a desk, a shirt. The bell holds the time.
Upakkilesa, stain or defilement. A dirty cloth won't take the dye; a mind washed of its stains takes the good.
Your line: clean cloth takes dye. Today, before you start something good, clear one small thing first: a grudge, a cluttered desk, an apology you owe. Day four hundred seven.

408.title: Effacement
408.hook: "others will be cruel; we will not be cruel here": forty-four resolves (MN 8)
408.howItsDone: Theravada teachers often use the Sallekha Sutta's refrain as a model for personal resolves, and monastic training emphasizes keeping one's own conduct whatever others around one do.

segments.voice: Yesterday: upakkilesa, and your line, clean cloth takes dye. Did you clear one small thing before starting something good? Day four hundred eight.

In almost any group there comes a moment when someone says: everyone does it. Everyone pads the expense report a little. Everyone talks about the boss when she's out of the room. Everyone's a bit cruel online; it's just how it works. It's hard to argue with, mostly because it's often true, at least a little. A discourse in the Middle-Length Sayings has an answer to it, set out forty-four times. Today: effacement.
screen: `EVERYONE DOES IT.` → `HARD TO ARGUE WITH.` → `AN ANSWER, FORTY-FOUR TIMES.`

segments.voice: MN 8, the Sallekha. A monk named Mahacunda asks how to let go of the many views people hold about the self and the world. The Buddha's answer begins somewhere unexpected. A monk might reach the deep meditative states, the jhanas, and think he's effacing. He isn't, the Buddha says. They're pleasant abidings, peaceful abidings, here and now. Effacement is something else. Sallekha comes from a verb meaning to scrape away, to pare down: the slow whittling of what doesn't belong. And then comes the refrain. Others will be cruel; we will not be cruel here: that is how you should efface. Others will kill living beings; we won't. Others will take what isn't given; we won't. Others will speak falsely, maliciously, harshly, idly; we won't. Others will be envious, stingy, deceitful, arrogant, hard to correct; we won't. Others will cling to their own views and let them go only with difficulty; we won't. Forty-four in all. Two things stand out. The refrain doesn't condemn the others. It never adds: and they're terrible. It says: here, among us, this is how we'll be. It draws a line around your own conduct. And it doesn't wait for everyone else to agree first. The Buddha gives a picture: just as there might be an uneven road, and another, even road to go around it, so not being cruel is the even road around cruelty. And the sutta ends with a line he repeats to many students: here are the roots of trees, here are empty huts. Meditate. Don't delay, or you'll regret it later.
screen: `JHANAS ARE NOT EFFACEMENT.` · `SALLEKHA — PARING DOWN.` · `OTHERS WILL; WE WON'T, HERE.` · `THE EVEN ROAD AROUND.` · then, large: `OTHERS MAY, WE WON'T.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the refrain run quietly, one line per breath. Others may be harsh; I won't be harsh here. Others may gossip; I won't gossip here. Others may cling to their views; I won't cling here. Let one of them land, the one that fits your week. Then drop the words, and just sit with that one resolve, like a smooth stone in your pocket. The bell holds the time.
Sallekha. Effacement: paring away what's unhelpful, line by line, whatever others are doing.
Your line: others may, we won't. Today, when you hear everyone does it, quietly keep your one resolve anyway. Day four hundred eight.

409.title: Sariputta on right view
409.hook: right view traced through nutriment, the truths and each link of the chain (MN 9)
409.howItsDone: Theravada monastics study the Sammaditthi Sutta as a systematic account of right view, and Sariputta is honored across Buddhist traditions as the disciple foremost in wisdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sallekha, and your line, others may, we won't. Did you keep your one resolve when everyone around you didn't? Day four hundred nine.

Good teachers have a move. They answer your question, and then wait to see whether you'll ask a better one. In MN 9, a group of monks keeps asking the same question, over and over, and their teacher, who for once isn't the Buddha, keeps finding a new answer. Sixteen answers to one question, each one going a little deeper, and the monks never seem to get tired of asking. Today: Sariputta on right view.
screen: `ONE QUESTION.` → `SIXTEEN ANSWERS.` → `NOT THE BUDDHA, THIS TIME.`

segments.voice: Sariputta was one of the Buddha's two chief disciples, known above all for wisdom; later commentaries call him the general of the teaching. In MN 9 he asks the monks: in what way is someone of right view? And he answers: when they understand the unwholesome and its root, and the wholesome and its root. The roots of the unwholesome are greed, hatred and delusion; the roots of the wholesome are their absence. The monks say: good, friend. But might there be another way? And he answers again. Nutriment: understanding the four kinds of food that keep beings going, their origin, their ending, and the way to their ending. Might there be another way? Dukkha, its origin, its ending, the way. Another? Aging and death, and their origin, and their ending, and the way. Then birth. Then being, clinging, craving, feeling, contact, the six senses, name and form, consciousness, formations, ignorance, and at last the taints. Sixteen rounds. Did you hear the pattern? From the second round on, every round takes the same four steps: this thing, where it comes from, where it ends, and the way there. It's the four noble truths used as a lens, and you can turn the lens on anything. That's what right view means in this discourse: less a belief to hold than a way of looking. Trace anything back far enough and you find a link in a chain. And links, the discourse says, can be undone.
screen: `SARIPUTTA, KNOWN FOR WISDOM.` · `MIGHT THERE BE ANOTHER WAY?` · `SIXTEEN ROUNDS, ONE PATTERN.` · `THING, ORIGIN, ENDING, WAY.` · then, large: `SARIPUTTA TEACHES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and pick one feeling that's here right now: restlessness, a little sadness, an ache. Try Sariputta's four steps on it, slowly. This is the feeling. Where did it come from: a thought, a contact, something someone said? When does it ease? What helps it ease? You don't need to finish the whole chain. One link is enough. Then let the steps go, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Samma-ditthi, right view. The chief disciple shows right view as a way of looking: each thing, its origin, its ending, and the way.
Your line: Sariputta teaches. Today, when something bothers you, ask his four questions once: what is it, where did it come from, when does it end, and what's the way? Day four hundred nine.

410.title: The lion's roar
410.hook: only here are the four kinds of noble ones, the Buddha roars (MN 11)
410.howItsDone: Buddhists across schools use the lion's roar, sihanada, as an image for confident teaching, and the lion appears widely in Buddhist art; the four stages of awakening are central to Theravada teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma-ditthi, and your line, Sariputta teaches. Did you try his four questions on something that bothered you? Day four hundred ten.

In the old Indian texts, a lion's roar isn't a snarl at anyone. It's an announcement: here I am, this is my ground, and I'm not afraid to say so. The phrase came to mean a bold, unhedged claim, made out loud and in public. The Buddha's discourses contain several lion's roars, and two of them sit side by side in the Middle-Length Sayings. MN 11 is the shorter one. Today: the lion's roar.
screen: `HERE I AM.` → `THIS IS MY GROUND.` → `A CLAIM MADE OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: MN 11 is the Culasihanada, the shorter discourse on the lion's roar. The Buddha tells his monks that they may rightly roar: only here is there a recluse, a second recluse, a third and a fourth. The Pali word is samana, a wandering renunciant. The commentaries read the four as the four stages of awakening: the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner and the arahant. It's a strong claim, and the text expects it to be challenged. What's interesting is what comes next. The Buddha expects that wanderers from other schools will ask: what's your basis for saying so? And he gives his monks an answer built from four things in their own lives: confidence in the Teacher, confidence in the teaching, the precepts fulfilled, and companions in the practice who are dear and agreeable. He then goes on to the question of clinging: to sense pleasures, to views, to rules and rituals, and to a doctrine of self, and says a teaching should make clear how each kind of clinging is understood. Notice the shape of it. The roar isn't volume. It isn't bravado. A lion roars because it knows its ground. You may remember the quail standing on its own clod a couple of weeks ago: same idea, louder. The confidence in this discourse rests on what the monks have actually lived: their trust, their practice, their friendships. A roar that rests on nothing is just noise.
screen: `SIHANADA — A BOLD CLAIM.` · `FOUR RECLUSES, ONLY HERE.` · `WHAT'S YOUR BASIS?` · `A LION KNOWS ITS GROUND.` · then, large: `A LION'S ROAR.`

segments.voice: Sit, and look for one thing you're actually sure of. Not something you've only been told, and not a grand claim about the universe. Something you've tested yourself: that a slow breath calms you, that a kind word lands better than a harsh one, that a short walk clears your head. Find it. Then, quietly, inside, say it once, plainly, with no maybe. Rest on it, the way the lion rests on its ground. The bell holds the time.
Sihanada, a lion's roar. A bold claim, made out loud, by someone who knows the ground they're standing on.
Your line: a lion's roar. Today, say one thing you've tested and are sure of, plainly, without hedging, to someone who'd want to hear it. Day four hundred ten.

411.title: Pleasure, danger, escape
411.hook: the gratification, the danger and the way out of sense pleasure (MN 13)
411.carry: the escape is from the hook
411.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers use the triad of gratification, danger and escape as a way of reflecting on desires; the lay precepts ask for restraint in sense pleasures rather than renouncing them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sihanada, and your line, a lion's roar. Did you say one thing you're sure of, plainly, to someone? Day four hundred eleven.

Every app store page has the same layout. What it does. The screenshots. The five-star reviews from people who love it. Almost none has a section called: what this will cost you. And none has a third section: how to stop using it when you want to. MN 13 asks for all three, about sense pleasure. Not to ruin the pleasure. To see the whole of it, plainly, before deciding. Today: pleasure, danger, escape.
screen: `WHAT IT DOES.` → `WHAT IT COSTS.` → `HOW TO STOP.`

segments.voice: MN 13, the Greater Discourse on the Mass of Suffering. The Buddha looks at sense pleasure in three ways. In Pali: assada, adinava, nissarana. The gratification, the danger, the escape. Gratification first, and he doesn't deny it. The pleasure and joy that arise from the five cords of sense pleasure, sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches, are real, he says. That's the gratification. Then the danger. A person earns a living by a trade: counting, accounting, farming, trading, herding, archery, service to the king. They face cold and heat, gadflies and mosquitoes, hunger and thirst. If their work fails, they grieve: all my effort was for nothing. If it succeeds, they worry: kings, thieves, fire or flood could take it, or an heir could squander it. And then the larger danger: for the sake of pleasures, kings quarrel with kings, nobles with nobles, householders with householders. Mother quarrels with son, son with mother, brother with sister, friend with friend. Then the escape: the removal of desire and lust for sense pleasures. Not the removal of every joy. In MN 36, the Buddha says he came to see that the joy of deep meditation wasn't something to fear. The escape is from the hook, not from happiness. Seeing all three is the whole method. The sutta says that anyone who doesn't see the gratification as gratification, the danger as danger and the escape as escape can't fully understand sense pleasures, let alone guide someone else. He applies the same three to the body and to feelings, too.
screen: `ASSADA — THE GRATIFICATION.` · `ADINAVA — THE DANGER.` · `NISSARANA — THE ESCAPE.` · `ALL THREE, OR YOU'RE HOOKED.` · then, large: `PLEASURE, DANGER, ESCAPE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one pleasure you love: coffee, a show, scrolling, a certain food. Give it its due first: notice the real enjoyment in it, even now, in memory. Then name its danger, plainly, without shame: what it costs in time, money, sleep or peace. Then touch the third, lightly: what would it be like to enjoy it without needing it? You don't have to give anything up. Just see all three. The bell holds the time.
Pleasure. In MN 13, sense pleasure is seen three ways: its gratification, its danger, and the way out.
Your line: the escape is from the hook. Today, before one small pleasure, say the three words to yourself, and then enjoy it. Day four hundred eleven.

412.title: Wildernesses of the heart
412.hook: five barren places in the heart: doubt about teacher, teaching, community, training, and anger at companions (MN 16)
412.howItsDone: Buddhist communities often encourage practitioners to bring doubts to a teacher rather than leave them unspoken, and the monastic rule sets out procedures for settling disputes between members.

segments.voice: Yesterday: pleasure, and your line, the escape is from the hook. Did you say the three words before one small pleasure, and then enjoy it anyway? Day four hundred twelve.
screen: `PLEASURE — THE ESCAPE IS FROM THE HOOK.`

segments.voice: A farmer can buy the best seed in the world, and if the field is full of stones and old stumps, not much comes up. Before planting, you clear the ground. It's slow, heavy work, with nothing to show for it yet. The Buddha described five patches of barren, stony ground in the heart, and five things that tie it down, and said the practice won't grow until they're dealt with. Today: wildernesses of the heart.
screen: `THE BEST SEED.` → `A FIELD FULL OF STONES.` → `CLEAR THE GROUND FIRST.`

segments.voice: MN 16, the Cetokhila. Ceto means heart or mind. Khila is harder to pin down: translators render it barrenness, wasteland, or a stake, something hard and stiff driven into the ground. Either way, it's ground that won't take seed. The five are these. Doubt about the Teacher. Doubt about the teaching. Doubt about the community. Doubt about the training. And the fifth: anger at your companions in the practice, being displeased and resentful toward them. Notice that last one. It isn't about doctrine at all. Being irritated with the people you practice alongside can make the ground as barren as any doubt. Then come five shackles that bind the heart: desire for sense pleasures, attachment to the body, attachment to outward forms, eating your fill and then indulging in sleep and lying around, and living the spiritual life only to be reborn among the gods. And then a picture for what happens when the field is cleared. A hen has eight or ten or twelve eggs. She sits on them, keeps them warm, turns them properly. Even if no wish arises in her, may my chicks break out safely with their claws and beaks, they'll hatch anyway. Clear the ground and do the patient work, and the result comes, whether you wish for it or not. In the sutta, the hen's patient work stands for fifteen things: the five wildernesses cleared, the five shackles cut, four bases of spiritual power developed, and enthusiasm. The eggs are warmed, not forced.
screen: `KHILA — BARREN, STONY GROUND.` · `FOUR DOUBTS AND ONE ANGER.` · `FIVE SHACKLES.` · `THE HEN AND HER EGGS.` · then, large: `CLEAR THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: Sit, and look over the field honestly. Is there a doubt that's gone hard and stony: about a teacher, a practice, a community you belong to? Or is it the fifth one, irritation with someone who shares a path with you? Pick one patch. You don't need to solve it. Just loosen it a little: breathe with it, the way a hen sits warmly on her eggs. The bell holds the time.
Cetokhila, barrenness of the heart. Five barren places, four doubts and anger at your companions, cleared so the practice can grow.
Your line: clear the field. Today, clear one stony patch: ask the question you've been doubting about, or soften toward one companion. Day four hundred twelve.

413.title: The honeyball
413.hook: Mahakaccana explains a short teaching: how perception spins out into endless thoughts (MN 18)
413.howItsDone: Theravada teachers often use Mahakaccana's sequence in MN 18 to explain how experience becomes thought; many meditators practice noticing contact and feeling before thinking takes over.

segments.voice: Yesterday: cetokhila, and your line, clear the field. Did you loosen one stony patch, a doubt or an irritation? Day four hundred thirteen, the end of the week.

A Sakyan named Dandapani, whose name means stick-in-hand, comes strolling up to the Buddha, leaning on his walking stick, and asks: what's your teaching? The Buddha answers in a sentence or two. Dandapani shakes his head, wags his tongue, raises his eyebrows until his forehead wrinkles in three lines, and walks off, still leaning on his stick. Some teachings don't land the first time. This one needed someone to unpack it. Today: the honeyball.
screen: `STICK-IN-HAND ASKS A QUESTION.` → `A SHORT ANSWER.` → `THREE LINES ON HIS FOREHEAD.`

segments.voice: MN 18, the Madhupindika. That evening, the Buddha repeats a short, dense teaching to his monks, about how perceptions and notions shaped by mental proliferation press in on a person, and then he gets up and goes into his dwelling. The monks look at each other: what did he mean? They go to Mahakaccana, a monk known for unpacking brief sayings. And he lays it out, step by step. Dependent on the eye and a form, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact, there's feeling. What you feel, you perceive. What you perceive, you think about. What you think about, you proliferate. And from that, a cloud of perceptions and notions, about past, present and future, presses in on you. The Pali word is papanca: spreading out, proliferation. You've watched it happen. A friend doesn't reply to a message, and five minutes later you've written their whole side of an argument they've never had. The monks take Mahakaccana's explanation back to the Buddha, who says: Mahakaccana is wise; I would have explained it the same way. And Ananda says: it's like a hungry man who finds a honeyball, a honey cake; wherever he tastes it, it's sweet. What is this teaching called? The Buddha says: remember it as the Honeyball. And so a week closes: the stained cloth, effacement, Sariputta's sixteen rounds, the lion's roar, pleasure seen whole, the stony field, and the honeyball.
screen: `A SHORT TEACHING, UNPACKED.` · `CONTACT, FEELING, PERCEPTION, THOUGHT.` · `PAPANCA — THE THOUGHTS MULTIPLY.` · `SWEET WHEREVER YOU TASTE IT.` · then, large: `THE HONEYBALL.`

segments.voice: Sit, and wait for a thought, any thought. When one comes, don't push it away. Watch what it does next: does it bring a friend? A plan, a memory, a what-if? See if you can catch the moment one thought becomes three. You don't need to stop it. Just say inside, quietly: spreading. Then come back to the breath and the body, to contact, before the story. The bell holds the time.
The honeyball. Mahakaccana's step-by-step map of how one sight or sound spreads into endless thoughts.

original.note: Pali papañca: proliferation, spreading out; how one perception multiplies into many thoughts.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sweet name for a sermon.
what it means: a map of how contact becomes feeling, feeling becomes thought, and thought spreads.

what a scholar hears: papañca is a famously hard word, rendered proliferation, diffuseness or mental elaboration; Mahākaccāna's chain runs eye, form, consciousness, contact, feeling, perception, thinking, proliferation.
